metaDescription: Five leaf blowers at or under $300, including an 80V Greenworks and brushless 40V options, compared on voltage, battery size and gas-replacement claims.
expertTake: The Greenworks 80V is the pick for anyone trying to retire a gas blower, since high voltage is what lets a battery tool approach gas-class output. The MTKOALA brushless kit is the value choice for a strong claimed number without a platform commitment. If you only sweep hard surfaces, this band is more tool than you need.
introParagraphs: At the top of the handheld cordless range, the goal is replacing a gas blower, not just tidying a patio. Higher voltage, brushless motors and bigger packs are the ingredients that make that plausible.

The honest questions are how much real air you get from a battery tool, and whether the pack is large enough to finish a lot in one session. Prices move, and the $300 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: Greenworks 80V Brushless Blower 700 CFM 2.5Ah
products.description:
The 80V system is the main reason this blower leads the group. Electrical power is volts times amps, so an 80V pack can deliver high wattage at a manageable current, and the brushless motor turns that into a fan speed a 20V tool cannot match. Greenworks pitches it against a 27cc gas blower, and while that comparison is a marketing frame rather than a standard measure, a 700 CFM claim on 80V hardware is far more credible than the same number from a 20V kit.

The pack is only 2.5Ah, but at 80V that stores much more energy than 2.5Ah at 20V, which is why a quick glance at amp hours alone misleads. Compared with the 40V Greenworks at 550 CFM, you get more airflow and a higher platform, but fewer amp hours, so a long session may need a second battery.

Ownership is easier than gas: no mixing fuel, no carburetor cleaning, no pull cord. Store the pack indoors, keep the intake clear and register the warranty. It is the right pick for a larger suburban lot. At this tier, think about the second battery before the blower: a spare 80V pack is a real purchase, so price the full setup you need for your lot instead of the tool alone. Many owners find that one pack covers a typical evening cleanup, while a long weekend session wants two.
products.bestFor: Owners replacing a gas handheld blower.
pros: Highest credible airflow claim in the group
cons: Small 2.5Ah pack may need a spare for long jobs
80V tools cost more to expand into

products.name: Greenworks 40V Brushless Blower 550 CFM 4.0Ah
products.description:
This 40V Greenworks pairs a brushless motor with a larger 4.0Ah pack, which makes it the more practical choice for a medium lot. The 550 CFM claim is lower than the 80V's 700, but the larger pack at a lower voltage still gives a respectable amount of working time.

The 40V family is broad, so the same pack can power mowers, trimmers and saws. That makes it the better buy for anyone who plans to own several cordless tools from one maker. The tradeoff is that it is not a gas-class blower; it is a very capable homeowner tool.

Keep an eye on charge time with a 4.0Ah pack, and store it partly charged over winter. It is the balanced choice for a typical suburban yard. If you already run a Greenworks trimmer or mower, the pack from that tool may fit this one, so check the compatibility chart before you buy a duplicate battery. Greenworks 40V packs share a family, so the blower becomes a cheap add-on rather than a new system.
products.bestFor: Typical suburban lots on a shared battery family.
pros: Part of a broad 40V tool family
Good balance of airflow and run time

products.name: MTKOALA 1200W Brushless Blower 700 CFM 200 MPH
products.description:
MTKOALA advertises a 1200W brushless motor with 700 CFM and 200 MPH, matching the Greenworks 80V on airflow and exceeding it on speed. The wattage figure is a motor input rating, and in a battery tool it is a peak, so treat the numbers as upper bounds.

The appeal is a high claimed output without committing to a platform. The tradeoff is that you are relying on an unfamiliar brand for support and replacement packs, which matters when the first pack fades.

Three speeds provide basic control. Charge according to the instructions, store the pack cool and expect to buy a replacement pack as it ages. It is the choice for someone who wants maximum claimed airflow and accepts the support risk. Because the brand is unfamiliar, keep the receipt and photograph the model label, which is what a support team will ask for in the first year. Check whether the replacement pack is sold separately before you commit, since that is the part most likely to fail first.
products.bestFor: High claimed output without a platform commitment.
pros: Highest air speed claim in the group
cons: Wattage and airflow are peak claims
Unknown brand means thin parts support

products.name: CRAFTSMAN V20 RP Cordless Blower 110 MPH
products.description:
The CRAFTSMAN is the lightest and least powerful pick at this ceiling, with a 110 MPH claim and a battery from the common V20 family. It is not competing with the 80V Greenworks on output; it is competing on convenience and shared batteries.

Its value is for households that own V20 drills and saws already. A battery you own means the blower is cheap to add, and replacement packs are widely stocked.

Keep it as a patio and driveway tool, and move to the 40V or 80V for leaves. Store the pack cool. Treat it as a light finishing tool: sweep the porch, steps and short drive, then reach for a stronger machine for the lawn. Its value is that it costs little to add if the batteries are already in your garage.
products.bestFor: V20 owners wanting a quick patio blower.
pros: Uses the widely stocked V20 battery family
Promises longer run time than earlier models
cons: Much lower airflow than the platform leaders

products.name: MZK 20V Cordless Blower 2 x 4.0Ah Kit
products.description:
The MZK is the budget anchor in a list otherwise built on higher voltage. It offers two 4.0Ah packs and a charger in a light body, aimed at patio and small lawn cleanup.

Compared with the Greenworks 80V, its voltage class limits output, so it will not clear a heavy leaf drop. What it offers is a cheap, swappable two-pack kit.

Store packs cool and partly charged. It suits a smaller yard where the premium tools would be overkill. With the smaller body and plain controls, it is easy to hand to a family member who finds a larger blower intimidating, and the second pack means the job rarely stops halfway.
products.bestFor: Small yards on a tight budget.
cons: No tool family behind the battery

buyingCriteria.explanation: Power is volts times amps, so higher voltage packs deliver more watts at lower current. The Greenworks 80V can sustain output that a 20V MZK cannot, despite similar claimed numbers on some listings. If gas replacement is the goal, buy the highest voltage you can afford. Add a quick sanity check: a large voltage number with a tiny pack still ends a long session early, so balance the two. This is also why a high-voltage tool feels more consistent from the first minute to the last, with less obvious power fade near the end of a charge, compared with a low-voltage kit.

A 2.5Ah pack at 80V stores far more energy than a 4.0Ah pack at 20V, because energy equals volts times amp hours. Compare watt hours, not amp hours alone. The 80V Greenworks and 40V Greenworks illustrate this clearly. Use watt hours as the common currency when you compare tools from different families, and you will rarely be fooled by a flashy label.

Claims like outperforming a 27cc gas blower are marketing frames, not standards. Use them as hints about intent, then check voltage and motor type. The MTKOALA's 1200W label is a similar peak figure. If a maker leads with a gas comparison, look for a stated motor type and voltage next to it before you believe it.

Greenworks 80V and 40V packs run other tools, and CRAFTSMAN V20 is widely stocked. A standalone kit like the MTKOALA has no family. Platform value shows up in year three when you need a replacement pack. Ask whether the pack you want is available alone, because a family tool that sells packs separately keeps your costs down when one fails.

Both Greenworks and the MTKOALA use brushless motors, which run cooler and last longer. A brushed motor at this price would be a warning sign. Brushless is now standard at this price, so use it as a minimum bar rather than a selling point.

A large pack on a slow charger means long waits. If your lot takes more than one pack, plan a spare or a fast charger. A second charger is cheap insurance for a two-pack household, because it halves the wait between sessions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voltage class
howWeEvaluated.description: We graded each tool by platform voltage because it governs sustained power. The 80V Greenworks scored highest and the 20V kits lowest. This is the single strongest predictor of real performance. That ordering reflects how sustained output scales with voltage, not brand preference.

howWeEvaluated.title: Energy in the box
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted packs to watt hours where voltage was known. The 80V 2.5Ah pack outweighs the 20V 4.0Ah packs. Complete kits scored above bare tools. Where a listing gave only amp hours, we estimated relative energy by platform voltage and flagged the uncertainty.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claim realism
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared airflow claims to platform voltage. A 700 CFM claim on 80V was treated as credible, while the same on a lesser platform was treated cautiously. This is a spec-sheet comparison and relies on maker data plus engineering reasoning.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the range of tools sharing each pack. Greenworks and CRAFTSMAN scored higher than standalone brands. We discounted any figure that was impossible for the battery to sustain.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered parts, warranty and brand history. Owner feedback patterns on durability informed the final order. Reports of pack fade and charger failures weighed more heavily than cosmetic details.

cards.label: 80V
cards.text: The 80V Greenworks delivers more sustained power and airflow and suits large lots, but costs more and the pack is smaller in amp hours.

cards.label: 40V
cards.text: The 40V Greenworks has a bigger pack, a broader family and a lower price, but cannot match the 80V on output.

howToChoose.note: Pick 80V to replace gas; pick 40V for a balanced homeowner kit.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: High voltage, brushless motor and enough pack energy for your lot. Compare watt hours, not amp hours.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks 80V is the only pick built for that role, with the MTKOALA as the claim-heavy alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need a backpack blower for an acre or more, or longer single-pack runtime. Backpack units and larger packs sit above this cap.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your debris is light and your lot small. The MZK or CRAFTSMAN clears it.

maintenance.why: Extreme heat or cold shortens pack life. Charge in a moderate space. Do not leave the pack in a hot car or on a sunny windowsill, which accelerates aging.
Debris starves the fan and raises temperature. A soft brush and compressed air are enough.
Lithium cells age faster when stored full or empty.
A loose nozzle leaks air and wastes power.
Dust blocks cooling slots and heats the motor.

faq.q: Can a cordless blower really replace gas?
faq.a: On a typical suburban lot, an 80V brushless unit can. Large acreage or commercial use still favors gas or a backpack. The difference shows most when you work for twenty minutes or more.
Because amp hours depend on voltage. A small Ah pack at 80V stores more energy than a larger Ah pack at 20V. Most users see the motor outlast the first battery by several years.
Treat them as peak motor input, not sustained output. Check the voltage and pack behind the number. Spares go on sale in late summer, so buy early if you can.

faq.q: Do I need a spare battery?
faq.a: For lots over a quarter acre, yes. A single small pack ends a session early.
Motors outlast packs. Expect battery fade after several seasons.
